title: AFFAIRE ŠEČIĆ c. CROATIE
conclusion: Violation de l'art. 3;Aucune question distincte au regard de l'art. 8 ou 13;Violation de l'art. 14+3;Préjudice moral - réparation pécuniaire;Remboursement partiel frais et dépens
summary:
In the case of Šečić v. Croatia, the applicant, Mr. Šečić, is a Croatian national of Roma origin who brought a complaint against the Croatian state. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to racially motivated violence and the failure of authorities to provide effective protection and investigation. On the evening of 29 April 1999 in Zagreb, Mr. Šečić was collecting scrap metal with others when he was violently attacked by a group of unidentified men wielding wooden planks and shouting racist insults. He suffered multiple broken ribs and developed post-traumatic stress disorder, requiring ongoing psychiatric treatment. Despite repeated requests from his lawyer, the police investigation was slow and ineffective, with key witnesses not promptly interviewed and leads not fully pursued, particularly regarding the racial motivation behind the attack.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) in conjunction with Article 3. The Court found that Croatia had violated Article 3 by failing to conduct an effective investigation and further violated Article 14 taken with Article 3 by not adequately addressing the racist nature of the attack. The Court awarded Mr. Šečić compensation for non-pecuniary damage and partial costs.

This judgment is significant as it highlights the obligation of states to protect Roma and Travellers from racially motivated violence and to investigate such crimes with particular diligence, reflecting a broader European context of persistent discrimination against these communities.
